text: SEC EDGAR enforces its fair-access policy: a User-Agent carrying a repo URL gets a flat 403, the same request with a contact email returns 200. EDGAR is therefore gated on settings.sec_enabled() (STOCKY_SEC_CONTACT) and skips itself when unset.

Bing News RSS answers a multi-term OR query with an EMPTY feed where Google News returns a full one. Bing needs a single quoted phrase plus 'stock' (services/news/bing_news.build_query); it cannot share google_news.build_query.

GDELT rejected as a news source: phrase search too loose ("shell" returns awards shows and retirement advice), legal suffix absent from body copy so the precise form finds nothing, ~20s TLS handshake and 429 at 1 req/5s. Cost more latency than all other sources combined for articles the relevance filter dropped. Bing covers the non-US reach instead.

Nasdaq's per-ticker RSS (www.nasdaq.com/feed/rssoutbound?symbol=X) returns GENERIC market news for unknown symbols rather than an empty feed - same trap as Yahoo's symbol-keyed endpoints. Keep NASDAQ out of dedup._RELATED_ALLOWED.

Nasdaq quote API splits a quote into primaryData (trading now, extended hours after the bell) and secondaryData (regular close). Use the regular-session block whenever present, else an after-hours print gets stored as the day's close. Also refuse suffixed symbols - SHEL.L would return the NY ADR.

Only about 5% of stored articles carry an image: most arrive via a Google News redirect, which services/news/images.py skips because resolving one costs a request and rarely yields an og:image, and STOCKY_IMAGE_FETCH_LIMIT caps fetches at 12 per stock per refresh. Any UI that leads with a picture must pick the first article that has one rather than the top-ranked article, or the hero slot is empty most of the time.

News feed diversity is not enforced server-side. marketbeat.com posts a near-identical 'X acquires N shares of NVIDIA' filing story every few minutes, so ORDER BY publish_time DESC returns ten of them in a row. The frontend caps per-source and per-symbol counts when rendering its recency column; if a second wire starts doing the same under rotating domains the fix belongs in services/dedup.py, not the client.

Killing the uvicorn reloader on Windows orphans its worker, which keeps port 5000. main.py runs reload=True, so there is a StatReload parent plus a multiprocessing.spawn worker that owns the listening socket. Kill only the parent and the worker survives, still serving the code it started with. netstat keeps listing the dead parent PID, so Get-Process on that PID reports no such process and it looks like an unkillable zombie socket. It is not: enumerate python.exe via Get-CimInstance Win32_Process, keep those whose CommandLine contains multiprocessing-fork and whose ParentProcessId no longer exists, and Stop-Process them. Filtering processes by CommandLine containing 'stocky' will NOT find them, because the worker command line is bare multiprocessing.spawn with no project path in it. No reboot and no port change are needed.

Yahoo's autocomplete endpoint (v1/finance/search, already wrapped by services.yahoo.search) returns sector and industry on every EQUITY quote, so symbol resolution captures the classification for free with no extra request. Use it rather than quoteSummary/assetProfile, which now demands a crumb. ETFs and indices come back null on both fields and are genuinely unclassifiable. Stocks resolved before the sector column existed short-circuit ensure_resolved because yahoo_symbol is already cached, so prices.ensure_classified re-runs just the search half with validate=False to backfill them.

Sector filtering needs both of Yahoo's levels, not one. The coarse 'sector' column is eleven buckets wide, so Rocket Lab sits in Industrials beside lift manufacturers and cannot express 'space stocks'. The precise 'industry' column says Aerospace & Defense but is so narrow that a twelve-stock watchlist yields ten filters holding one stock each. /stocks/sectors returns both tagged with a level field, and db.stocks.symbols_in_sector matches either column.

Postgres queries here use %s placeholders, never ?. Search columns must use ILIKE, not LIKE: SQLite matched ASCII case-insensitively and Postgres does not, so a straight LIKE port silently makes /stocks/search and the news query case-sensitive and they go quiet for lowercase input.

db.news.insert_news_many chunks at 500 rows because Postgres caps a statement at 65535 bind parameters and the multi-row INSERT binds 16 per article - 4095 rows. A month-long backfill of a well-covered ticker can reach that, and the failure is an opaque OperationalError from the driver, not a SQL error.

There is no migration framework: the schema is one CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS block in db/connection.py, run under pg_advisory_xact_lock so the API and scheduler can start simultaneously. A column change means editing that block and applying the ALTER by hand. The SQLite era's self-migrating ALTER/backfill machinery was deleted with the port; import_sqlite.py replaced it as a one-shot.

Tests run against a real Postgres (stocky_test, TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY per test via the temp_db fixture), not a SQLite stand-in. That is deliberate: a stand-in would stop the suite catching dialect mistakes, which is the whole class of bug the port introduced. STOCKY_TEST_DSN overrides the target and that database is wiped.

The live SQLite schema declared news.AI_summary with legacy capitals. SQLite resolves column names case-insensitively so every query worked, but SELECT * returned the key as 'AI_summary' while routes/schemas.py and services/ai_service.py both read row.get('ai_summary') - so cached per-article AI summaries were written and never read back, and DeepSeek was re-billed on every request. Postgres folds identifiers to lowercase, which fixes it. Any future SQLite import must match column names case-insensitively or it silently drops the column.

Verify a storage-engine port with a differential harness, not just the unit suite: check the old db module out of git, point it at a copy of the old database, run both modules through the same calls and diff the results. It caught two things 429 passing tests did not - a dropped column and unstable ORDER BY on ties. Compare serialised JSON rather than Python equality, or 0 vs False and int vs Decimal hide real key-name differences.

Orderings in db/news.py must end in a unique tiebreaker. source_breakdown, count_by_stock, get_unscored and get_missing_images ordered on a non-unique column alone; SQLite happened to return ties in rowid order and Postgres does not, so the same query returned different rows between two calls. The file's own header comment already stated the convention - it just was not applied everywhere.

Surrogate keys are UUIDv7 via Postgres 18's built-in uuidv7() as the column DEFAULT - no extension, no Python-side generation. This pins the minimum server version to PG 18; there is no fallback and the failure on an older server is 'function uuidv7() does not exist'. v7 over v4 because the timestamp occupies the leading bytes, so ids sort chronologically, inserts stay at the right edge of the B-tree, and ORDER BY publish_time DESC, id DESC remains a meaningful tiebreaker.
Article ids are UUIDs, so GET/POST /news/{news_id} returns 422 for an unparseable id where the old integer route returned 404. A well-formed but absent id is still 404. Tests pin both.

Changing a column type does not take effect on an existing database: the schema is CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, so an already-created table is left untouched and the app runs on the old shape while the tests fail confusingly. DROP the tables (or the database) and re-run create_tables, then re-import. Applies to the test database too - stocky_test needs the same drop.
